# Song of Solomon 5: Research Notes

**Limits of these notes:**
- **No Catholic or Orthodox material.** I didn't reach any pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, so that section is missing. The only Jewish and Patristic views below come second-hand through Protestant commentators.
- **No prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching.** I found nothing tied to this chapter, so that is left out.
- **Only one modern-scholarship source.** That is the NET Bible notes. I didn't reach bibleodyssey.org.
- **The Enduring Word page was cut off** after v. 8 when I fetched it. Its notes on vv. 9–16 come only from search snippets.
- **I didn't read the full Gill or Henry commentaries.** Their points come from page snippets.

**Main dividing line:** The real split is not between denominations. It is between two ways of reading the Song. One reads it as an allegory of Christ and the church: Wesley (Methodist), Gill and Spurgeon (Baptist), Matthew Henry. The other reads it mainly as a poem about married love: Guzik (Enduring Word), Patterson, Glickman, Constable, Longman. A few writers also argue over who the lover is, Solomon or a shepherd. Each point below gives its URL.

---

**v. 1**
- **Married-love reading:** Patterson sees three images: the fragrance of the couple's union, the sweetness of their relationship, and full satisfaction of sexual desire. Glickman reads the call to "eat… drink" as hearty approval of their wedding night. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_5
- **Against allegory:** Longman calls all the garden, honey and wine imagery the language of sexual intimacy, with the chorus celebrating it. The same page argues that allegory arose from the outlook that also produced monasticism, and that the Song teaches that sex in marriage is God's gift. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_5
- **Delitzsch:** The phrase "come into my garden" echoes the Hebrew idiom for a husband going in to his wife. He reads the verbs as looking back on the act, and says this enjoyment brings no regret because it stayed within God's order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-1.htm
- **Ellicott:** The margin reading "be drunken with loves" gives the right sense. The poet likes to invite others to share his joy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-1.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** This is the Bridegroom answering the church. The "pleasant fruits" are his people's service and obedience. The "friends" are believers, urged to enjoy their spiritual food freely. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Matthew Henry:** Christ is ready to accept his people's invitations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-1.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** This verse really belongs at the end of chapter 4, as Christ's answer to the church's request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-1.htm
- **Coffman (Church of Christ):** This celebrates the Shulamite's marriage to the Shepherd, not to Solomon, and pictures the church's marriage to Christ. Redford links the wine and milk to the free offer in Isaiah 55:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Pulpit Commentary (J.R. Thomson):** Marriage and feasting are joined here, as in Jesus' parables. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** Scholars disagree about who speaks the last lines, and the notes list five options. The plural form makes it unlikely that one spouse is addressing the other. The NET favours the poet, or the wedding guests addressed as if present. "Drink" compares getting drunk on wine with enjoying a spouse's love (compare Proverbs 5:19–20). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?mode=print&passage=Song+of+Solomon+5:1-8:14

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** The woman is dreaming, or drifting between sleep and waking. Whether this comes before or after the wedding matters less than the trouble in the relationship. He counts five rising appeals: the lover's presence, his voice, his request, his tender names, and the hardship he endured to come. He notes that this scene may be behind Revelation 3:20. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Meaning of "perfect one":** Carr, quoted by Guzik, says the word means moral blamelessness rather than "virgin." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Barnes:** "I sleep, but my heart waketh" is a poetic way of saying "I dream." Barnes also reports that ancient allegorists read the chapter as Israel during the Babylonian exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-2.htm
- **Wesley:** "Asleep" means dull and sluggish, yet her thoughts were still on her beloved. Christ knocks by his word, providence and Spirit. The pile of tender names shows his love. The dew stands for his sufferings for the church. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Gill and Henry:** Gill reads the sleeping "I" and the waking heart as the two principles in the believer, sin and grace (compare Romans 7). Henry likewise sees corruption at work alongside grace that remains. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/5-2.html
- **Gill also:** Christ's knock may be the rod of affliction, used to shake the church out of complacency. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-2.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** He preached on this verse as a riddle: sleep admitted, wakefulness claimed. The heart is awake because it hears the Beloved's knock. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/asleep-and-yet-awake-a-riddle/
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** The line can mean either "I was dozing off when I was suddenly woken" or "I was asleep, but my mind was dreaming." The phrase "Listen! My lover" repeats 2:8. There she was eager; here she is indifferent. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?mode=print&passage=Song+of+Solomon+5:1-8:14

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** Her reply is only excuses. Carr hears petulant unwillingness, not real inability. The trouble is not that she never goes to the door but that she goes slowly, making excuses. Estes and Kinlaw use this to discuss the adjustments marriage requires. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Wesley:** Getting up again was inconvenient. Eastern people washed their feet before bed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** She has left her first love. Her repentance and restoration show both the single soul and the church in decline. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Tyndale (Carr):** This was a passing lapse, common in marriage, that could ruin a relationship if it continued. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_5

**v. 4**
- **Guzik:** The lover won't force the latch; he enters only if invited. Guzik discusses a possible double meaning ("hand" as a euphemism in Isaiah 57:8; "latch" literally "hole"). He judges it not the main sense, because the lover is outside. If present, it may hint at her own mixed longings. Carr, by contrast, thinks the sexual meaning is present here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Wesley:** When his word failed to move her, his Spirit, "the finger of God" (Luke 11:20), worked inwardly on her conscience. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** Translates "thrust his hand through the hole." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?mode=print&passage=Song+of+Solomon+5:1-8:14

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** The myrrh was the lover's "love note" (Glickman), left without anger. Guzik sees here a model for how a husband should answer disrespect. Clarke mentions an ancient custom of perfuming a bride's doors. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Wesley:** The myrrh dropped from the Bridegroom's hand onto the door. Though Christ withdrew, he left "a sweet savour" behind. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It is the lover's fragrance being celebrated, not hers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-5.htm
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Poole:** The myrrh stands for bitter repentance, and the lock handles for the sins that shut him out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-5.htm
- **Other explanations:**
  - Cambridge Bible: the wording suggests the myrrh came from her own hands; she had probably perfumed herself before bed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/songs/5.htm
  - Ellicott: a lover without a key might use soft myrrh to work the bolt's pins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/5.htm
- **Solomon or shepherd?** Delitzsch asks whether a country shepherd would bring oil of myrrh, and concludes the visitor is Solomon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/5-5.htm

**v. 6**
- **Guzik:** She was too late. Now the roles are reversed: she calls and gets no answer. Guzik quotes Taylor: here the bride lost her Bridegroom through lazy self-indulgence, not worldliness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Wesley:** Christ withheld his comforting presence as a just penalty for her neglect. She sought him "by diligent enquiry and importunate prayer." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Pulpit Commentary (Thomson):** The Saviour may withdraw to draw out stronger love, deeper repentance and more fervent prayer. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **BibleHub study notes:** His leaving pictures the fellowship believers miss when they ignore his prompting. https://biblehub.com/songs/5.htm

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** In a dream, the beating may reflect her guilt (Kinlaw). The "veil" is more likely a scarf or mantle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Other marriage-reading writers:**
  - Constable: she may have felt, deep down, that she deserved punishment.
  - Deere: the dream shows the pain of a separation her selfishness caused.
  - MacArthur, who reads it as a real event: in the dark, they may not have recognised the new bride.
  - The same page notes that the watchmen helped her in 3:3 but harm her here, and that the word for "bruised" means an open wound.

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_5
- **Wesley:** The watchmen are church leaders who should comfort the faithful but often discourage them. The blows are slanders and persecutions. Taking her veil treats her as if she had no tie to Christ. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Gill:** They took her for a night-walker. If they were true ministers, the "blows" were rebukes for her coldness to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/5-7.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** When the soul loses its joy in Christ, even the church's own guardians may misjudge it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Coffman:** The beating stands for the world's persecution of the church, and the wounds for martyrdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-5.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** This lovesickness differs from 2:5. There she was overwhelmed by love's presence; here she aches at its absence. Applying it spiritually, he quotes Spurgeon: the soul longs not for salvation but for present fellowship with Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Wesley:** She asks every believer she meets about him. "Tell him" means she is ready to faint without his presence. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/

**v. 9**
- **Wesley:** Believers might ask this so as to learn more about him. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Guzik (older study guide):** "Fairest among women" may be sarcastic, since she would look dishevelled after the search and the beating. Meyer says her anguish told them her lover was no ordinary man. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Sgs/Sgs_5.cfm
- **Ellicott:** This question makes it close to certain that the poem was sung by alternating choirs at a wedding. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/5.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** Pictures her telling the dream while still half awake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/songs/5.htm

**v. 10**
- **Wesley:** White means his spotless innocence; ruddy means his bloody passion. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Coffman:** Links the whiteness to the snow-white hair of Christ in Revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **BibleHub study notes:** The Hebrew word (*dagul*) uses military-banner imagery. https://biblehub.com/songs/5.htm
- **Guzik:** Watchman Nee applied each feature to Jesus, reading "white and ruddy" as perfect health and fullness of life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** Translates "dazzling and ruddy… stands out in comparison to all other men." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?mode=print&passage=Song+of+Solomon+5:1-8:14
- **Overall (vv. 10–16):** Guzik sees her rediscovering his worth, with the painful irony that she praises the man she was slow to let in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/

**v. 11**
- **Wesley:** His head shines because of a golden crown. Wesley then cautions against fitting each body part to some particular excellence of Christ, calling that guesswork. The point is simply that Christ is beautiful without flaw from head to foot. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/song-of-solomon-5.html

**v. 12**
- **Ellicott:** "Washed in milk" means the white of the eye. "Fitly set" may mean set like a gem in a ring. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/5.htm
- **Wesley:** Lovely, chaste and innocent; doves of milk-white colour. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/

**v. 13**
- **Ellicott:** Probably refers to a perfumed beard (compare Psalm 133:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/5.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** Refers to the perfume of his breath (compare 7:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/songs/5.htm
- **Wesley:** Spice beds please both sight and smell. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Songs.html

**v. 14**
- **Wesley:** Gold rings set with gems. "Belly" stands for his whole body. Sapphires are bright white with blue veins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/song-of-solomon-5.html

**v. 15**
- **Wesley:** Legs that are straight and strong. Feet bright like gold, as in Revelation 1:15. Tall and stately like Lebanon's cedars. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Guzik's study guide:** As Lebanon towers over the hills, he surpasses other men in stature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Sgs/Sgs_5.cfm

**v. 16**
- **Ellicott:** Literally "his palate is sweetness," meaning his voice and speech are exquisitely sweet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/5.htm
- **Wesley:** "Altogether" is her way of not going into more detail. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
- **Spurgeon:** He calls these words the bride's summary after her tenfold description, and says Jesus is lovely "cross and all." https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/altogether-lovely/
- **Spurgeon's verse expositions:** Each saint has some virtue, but all of them are found in Christ. "All desires" is also a good translation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Guzik:** Jesus is beautiful from every angle, yet the world hardly sees it. The verse also raises the question of why she was so slow to answer such a man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-5/
- **Kinlaw:** The Song is erotic but never content with the physical alone; her lover is also her friend. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_5
- **BibleHub study notes:** "My friend" echoes John 15:15. https://biblehub.com/songs/5.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** Translates "totally desirable… my companion." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?mode=print&passage=Song+of+Solomon+5:1-8:14

---

## Where readings differ, chapter-wide

- **Christ and the church:**
  - Wesley (Methodist) says the whole book is about Christ and his church, not Solomon and Pharaoh's daughter. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-song-of-solomon/
  - Gill and Spurgeon (Baptist) read it the same way. See the v. 2 and v. 16 links.
- **Married love:** Guzik, Patterson, Glickman and Longman. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_5
- **Shepherd reading:** Coffman thinks the absent lover must be the Good Shepherd, Christ, now in heaven, not Solomon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Israel reading (Brethren):** Arend Remmers, in the overview on the StudyLight Wesley page, reads the Song as the Jewish remnant and the Messiah. He sees 5:2–6:9 as "restoration of love." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/song-of-solomon.html
- **Jewish and early Christian readings (second-hand):** Coffman reports that Jewish interpreters read vv. 2–8 as the Babylonian captivity. He also reports that some early Christian interpreters read her sleep as the church's sluggishness after the great persecutions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-5.html
- **Poem or wedding songs (scholarship):** The Cambridge Bible argues against Budde's view that the Song is a collection of separate wedding songs, because this chapter has a connected storyline. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/songs/5.htm
